# ImgLoop

No sign-up · free online · privacy first

September 19, 2026 free online AI photo editor with local canvas and transparent AI credits

Hi Indie Hackers,

I'm building ImgLoop, a browser-based AI photo editor that opens without sign-up. The idea came from frustration with online editors that demand an account before you can even crop an image. I wanted a tool where you can upload a JPG, PNG, or WebP file up to 20 MB and start editing immediately.

Local tools like crop, rotate, brush, erase, and text run directly in the browser and cost 0 credits. Thanks for reading.

ImgLoop exists because editing photos online should be simple, private, and free to try. I wanted a browser editor where anyone can improve an image without signing up, with clear credit costs before any AI request.

Azuqe - Indie Hackers

# Azuqe

The OS for Reach

September 19, 2026 We’re building Azuqe an OS for reach

We started building Azuqe as an SEO platform.

But the more we worked on it, the more we realized that SEO is only one part of how a business gets discovered today.

People still search Google, but they also discover businesses through AI assistants, Reddit, YouTube, LinkedIn, Quora, Medium, communities, and other places across the web.

And this creates a messy problem for businesses.

You might have great content, but nobody sees it.

You might rank well on Google, but not appear in AI answers.

You might know exactly what content you need to create, but getting it distributed across the right channels is another problem.

You might discover an SEO issue, but fixing it requires another tool, another person, or a developer.

And suddenly, managing “SEO” means jumping between a dozen different platforms.

### That's why we're building Azuqe.

We think businesses need an OS for reach one place to manage how they get discovered across the modern web.

### Create

Azuqe helps you research keywords and topics, analyze competitors and search results, create content, optimize existing content, manage internal linking, and run your content workflow.

But we don't want content creation to mean “ask AI to write an article and publish it.”

Before generating content, Azuqe brings together search data, competitor research, search intent, ranking opportunities, related topics, and other signals to understand what people are actually looking for and what content has a chance of being useful.

The goal is content that is research-driven, useful, and human in how it communicates — not generic AI-generated text that loses the emotion and perspective that makes content worth reading.

### Distribute

This is one of the areas we're particularly excited about.

You can take an article, an idea, or a topic and create platform-specific content for:

- Reddit
- Quora
- LinkedIn
- Medium
- YouTube

The goal isn't to blindly post the same thing everywhere.

It's to make distribution part of the content workflow — while adapting content to each platform's norms and community rules rather than treating every channel like another place to dump links.

### Discover

Azuqe brings together the signals you need to understand where you're visible and where you're missing:

- Keyword rankings
- Technical SEO
- AI visibility
- AI citations
- Competitor visibility
- Backlinks
- Google Search Console
- Google Analytics
- Bing Webmaster Tools
- Traffic analytics

For AI visibility specifically, we don't just want to tell you:

> “Your brand isn't appearing.”

We want to help answer:

> Where are competitors being cited? What sources are influencing the answer? Where are the opportunities? What can you actually do about them?

### Execute

Finding an opportunity is only useful if you can act on it.

Azuqe can help identify technical SEO issues, recommend fixes, execute supported fixes through our website integration, generate implementation-ready changes through MCP, publish content, and automate indexing.

We're also building GitHub CI/CD workflows so SEO can become part of the development process instead of something checked after deployment.

### Connect

We don't want businesses to rebuild their existing stack around Azuqe.

That's why we're building integrations with platforms teams already use — including WordPress, Shopify, Webflow, Wix, Ghost, Framer, Blogger, Notion, Google Docs, Dev.to, Hashnode, GitHub and more.

### Automate

AIM is our AI execution layer.

Instead of just giving you another dashboard, AIM can work with your SEO and search data to answer questions, identify problems, generate content briefs, create content, recommend actions, trigger indexing, generate reports, and automate repetitive workflows.

The bigger idea is:

Create → Distribute → Get Discovered → Measure → Optimize → Repeat

We don't think the future of search is just about ranking a page on Google.

And we don't think the answer is just another AI visibility dashboard either.

The web is becoming increasingly fragmented.

Search engines. AI assistants. Communities. Social platforms. Video. Content platforms.

Businesses need a way to manage their reach across all of them.

That's what we're trying to build with Azuqe.

We're still early, and we're actively looking for founders, marketers, SEO teams, content teams, and agencies who are dealing with this problem.

I'd genuinely love to hear from you:

How are you currently managing your company's reach across all these different channels?

And if you're already using multiple tools for this, what feels the most painful or fragmented today?

Azuqe: https://azuqe.com/

body:
LazyWatch - Indie Hackers

# LazyWatch

Track what you watch. Find your people

September 18, 2026 We missed TV Time, so three friends built our own tracker

A few months ago, TV Time shut down.

I’d used it for years, so naturally I started trying alternatives. Some were great at tracking. Some were good for discovery. Others had social features. But none of them felt like the app I actually wanted to keep using.

So I messaged two friends and we decided to build our own.

At first, LazyWatch was really just for us. We wanted a place to track shows and movies, know when the next episode was coming out, and keep our watch history without making it feel like work.

Then we kept adding the things we personally wanted.

Episode comments, so you can talk about what just happened without digging through a random Reddit thread.

Ratings and reviews.

Swipes to find something for movie night or your next binge.

Upcoming episodes.

Stats.

Lists and Top 5s.

Imports, because nobody wants to manually rebuild years of watch history.

Eventually it stopped feeling like a side project and started feeling like an actual product.

The biggest lesson for me has been how different building is from talking about building.

You can spend forever thinking about the perfect UX, roadmap, or architecture, but once real people start using the app, your priorities change fast. Things you thought were important barely get touched. Tiny annoyances become obvious. Features you almost skipped end up becoming some of the most useful ones.

We’re still early, and there’s plenty we want to improve. But LazyWatch is now live on iOS, Android, and the web, which still feels a little strange considering it started because three people missed an app.

If you’re building something similar, the best thing we did was start with a problem we actually had ourselves.

And if you try LazyWatch, I’d genuinely love to hear what feels good, what feels off, and what you think we should build next.

## About

LazyWatch exists because TV Time shut down and none of the alternatives felt right. So three friends built the tracker we wanted ourselves, with tracking, discovery, upcoming episodes, and real show discussions.

The OS for Reach

September 19, 2026 We’re building Azuqe an OS for reach

We started building Azuqe as an SEO platform.

But the more we worked on it, the more we realized that SEO is only one part of how a business gets discovered today.

People still search Google, but they also discover businesses through AI assistants, Reddit, YouTube, LinkedIn, Quora, Medium, communities, and other places across the web.

And this creates a messy problem for businesses.

You might have great content, but nobody sees it.

You might rank well on Google, but not appear in AI answers.

You might know exactly what content you need to create, but getting it distributed across the right channels is another problem.

You might discover an SEO issue, but fixing it requires another tool, another person, or a developer.

And suddenly, managing “SEO” means jumping between a dozen different platforms.

### That's why we're building Azuqe.

We think businesses need an OS for reach one place to manage how they get discovered across the modern web.

### Create

Azuqe helps you research keywords and topics, analyze competitors and search results, create content, optimize existing content, manage internal linking, and run your content workflow.

But we don't want content creation to mean “ask AI to write an article and publish it.”

Before generating content, Azuqe brings together search data, competitor research, search intent, ranking opportunities, related topics, and other signals to understand what people are actually looking for and what content has a chance of being useful.

The goal is content that is research-driven, useful, and human in how it communicates — not generic AI-generated text that loses the emotion and perspective that makes content worth reading.

### Distribute

This is one of the areas we're particularly excited about.

You can take an article, an idea, or a topic and create platform-specific content for:

- Reddit
- Quora
- LinkedIn
- Medium
- YouTube

The goal isn't to blindly post the same thing everywhere.

It's to make distribution part of the content workflow — while adapting content to each platform's norms and community rules rather than treating every channel like another place to dump links.

### Discover

Azuqe brings together the signals you need to understand where you're visible and where you're missing:

- Keyword rankings
- Technical SEO
- AI visibility
- AI citations
- Competitor visibility
- Backlinks
- Google Search Console
- Google Analytics
- Bing Webmaster Tools
- Traffic analytics

For AI visibility specifically, we don't just want to tell you:

> “Your brand isn't appearing.”

We want to help answer:

> Where are competitors being cited? What sources are influencing the answer? Where are the opportunities? What can you actually do about them?

### Execute

Finding an opportunity is only useful if you can act on it.

Azuqe can help identify technical SEO issues, recommend fixes, execute supported fixes through our website integration, generate implementation-ready changes through MCP, publish content, and automate indexing.

We're also building GitHub CI/CD workflows so SEO can become part of the development process instead of something checked after deployment.

### Connect

We don't want businesses to rebuild their existing stack around Azuqe.

That's why we're building integrations with platforms teams already use — including WordPress, Shopify, Webflow, Wix, Ghost, Framer, Blogger, Notion, Google Docs, Dev.to, Hashnode, GitHub and more.

### Automate

AIM is our AI execution layer.

Instead of just giving you another dashboard, AIM can work with your SEO and search data to answer questions, identify problems, generate content briefs, create content, recommend actions, trigger indexing, generate reports, and automate repetitive workflows.

The bigger idea is:

Create → Distribute → Get Discovered → Measure → Optimize → Repeat

We don't think the future of search is just about ranking a page on Google.

And we don't think the answer is just another AI visibility dashboard either.

The web is becoming increasingly fragmented.

Search engines. AI assistants. Communities. Social platforms. Video. Content platforms.

Businesses need a way to manage their reach across all of them.

That's what we're trying to build with Azuqe.

We're still early, and we're actively looking for founders, marketers, SEO teams, content teams, and agencies who are dealing with this problem.

I'd genuinely love to hear from you:

How are you currently managing your company's reach across all these different channels?

And if you're already using multiple tools for this, what feels the most painful or fragmented today?

Azuqe: https://azuqe.com/

# Foca Upscaler

September 18, 2026 Higher resolution doesn’t always mean a better image

I've been working on Foca Upscaler for a while, and one problem kept coming back while testing low-resolution images:

Making an image sharper is easy. Recovering detail that is no longer there is much harder.

Traditional enhancement can clean up edges, reduce softness, and make an image look crisper. That works well when the original image already contains enough usable information.

But some images are simply missing too much detail.

A tiny face, compressed hair, fabric texture, or a blurred object doesn't suddenly contain more information just because you upscale it 4x.

That was the reason I added Physics mode to Foca.

Foca now has two different enhancement approaches.

Sharp is meant for images where the original structure is already there and mostly needs cleaner, clearer enlargement.

Physics is for images where more detail needs to be reconstructed rather than simply sharpened.

The interesting part is that reconstruction creates a completely different problem.

If you push it too far, the result can look impressive but stop being faithful to the original. Skin becomes too perfect. Fabric gains textures that may never have existed. Small details become sharper, but not necessarily more accurate.

So the goal with Physics isn't simply “generate as much detail as possible.”

It's to reconstruct enough detail to make a low-resolution image useful again without turning it into a different image.

That's also changed how I think about resolution.

Foca supports upscaling up to 16K, but 16K alone isn't a quality metric. If those extra pixels are filled with fake-looking detail, the larger image isn't really better.

For me, the harder problem is finding the point where reconstruction helps more than it hurts.

That's still one of the most interesting parts of building Foca.

If you want to see what I'm working on:

https://focaupscaler.com/

coverMyGame - Indie Hackers

# coverMyGame

September 19, 2026 Why I am building coverMyGame

Most platforms that connect game developers with creators ask for a subscriber count or a quality bar before you can use them properly. Those are fair rules that happen to lock out everybody who is starting. This is the one I wanted when I started, and what I am trying to do differently. There are already plenty of places where game developers and creators find each other, and most of them work. I am not here to tell you they are broken. I am here because I could not get through the door of any of them when I started, and I doubt I am the only one.

## The bar is invisible once you are over it

Look at what most of these platforms ask for before you can use them properly. A subscriber count. A channel that has been going a while. On the other side, a game that clears somebody’s quality bar, with a trailer that looks like it had a budget and a store page that looks like a studio wrote it.

None of that is unfair. If you are running a service at scale, thresholds are how you keep the quality up and the noise down, and every one of those rules was written for a good reason. The trouble is that they are invisible to everybody already past them, and they are the entire experience if you are not.

A developer shipping their first game has no reviews to point at. A creator on their second month has no subscriber count to clear a floor with. Both of them are exactly the people who would get the most out of finding each other, and both of them are the people the rules are written to filter out.

## I hit this from both sides

I am building a YouTube channel myself, and starting was harder than I expected. Not the making: the getting anywhere near the games. Every route to a developer wanted a number I did not have yet. And the same week I would read a post from somebody who had just shipped a first game asking, in earnest, how on earth you get anyone to look at it.

So this is not market research. I am building the tool I wanted to use, and if it is useful to other people starting out then that is the whole of the ambition. Everything in it exists because it annoyed me first.

## The other half: being reachable should not cost this much

The flip side of being hard to reach is being too easy to reach. Once one address of yours is out there, you get PDFs. You get press kits you did not ask for. You get the same letter eleven times from eleven people who all bought the same list, and a few that are not letters at all but somebody trying to get into your account.

And the honest bit, which nobody says out loud: sometimes I do not want to talk to anybody. I want to look at what is there, take the thing I am interested in, and get on with it. Having to open a conversation with a stranger before anything can happen is a real cost, and for a lot of people it is the cost that stops them.

## So you decide how much of this you want

This is the part I care most about getting right. How much contact you accept is a setting, not a character trait, and both extremes are supported on purpose.

- Say what you actually want sent, and nothing outside it reaches you. If that is nothing at all, that works too, and it costs you nothing to say so.
- You never have to negotiate. A creator can look through the games here and ask for a key; a developer can say yes or nothing. No pitch meeting, no small talk, no thread.
- Or talk properly, if that is what you like. Some of the best coverage comes out of two people actually getting on. The point is that it is a choice you make, not a toll you pay.

## A feedback loop that goes both ways

The thing missing from almost every version of this is what happens afterwards. A developer sends a key into the dark and never learns whether the video happened, whether it landed, or why not. A creator covers a game and never hears whether it moved anything.

Both sides get to say what worked here, and both sides get to read it. Two people getting better at this beats two people guessing at it, and over enough rounds that is the thing that makes a small channel and a small studio worth each other’s time.

## It is not unique, and that is fine

I want to be straight about this, because a launch post that claims to have invented something is the first sign that it has not. This is not a new idea. Plenty of people are doing a version of it, and several of them are doing it well.

If there were one car maker in the world we would all still be driving the same car. Things get better because somebody builds the version they wanted and other people turn out to want it too. So: no corporate look, no corporate rules, a low front door, and someone at the other end who answers. I am flexible, I will take feedback seriously, and I would rather change my mind in public than defend a decision I have gone off. What is not built yet

It would be easy to write all of that as though the thing were finished. It is not, and pretending otherwise would break the first rule on the card above.

- I do think about how this pays for itself one day, but none of that is built: no checkout, no billing page, nothing to buy. Use the whole thing for free while that is true.
- I am still running interviews with developers and creators, and the answers still change what gets built next.

## Come and punk your way through this with me

That is genuinely how this feels: no publisher, no permission, no waiting to be picked. Building the room I wanted to be in, and leaving the door open.

Accounts are not open yet. Leave an address on the waiting list and I will write when they are. I may ask you for a short interview before then, and nothing else.

People still search Google, but they also discover businesses through AI assistants, Reddit, YouTube, LinkedIn, Quora, Medium, communities, and other places across the web.

And this creates a messy problem for businesses.

You might have great content, but nobody sees it.

You might rank well on Google, but not appear in AI answers.

You might know exactly what content you need to create, but getting it distributed across the right channels is another problem.

You might discover an SEO issue, but fixing it requires another tool, another person, or a developer.

We think businesses need an OS for reach one place to manage how they get discovered across the modern web.

Azuqe helps you research keywords and topics, analyze competitors and search results, create content, optimize existing content, manage internal linking, and run your content workflow.

But we don't want content creation to mean “ask AI to write an article and publish it.”

Before generating content, Azuqe brings together search data, competitor research, search intent, ranking opportunities, related topics, and other signals to understand what people are actually looking for and what content has a chance of being useful.

You can take an article, an idea, or a topic and create platform-specific content for:

- LinkedIn

The bigger idea is:

Create → Distribute → Get Discovered → Measure → Optimize → Repeat

The web is becoming increasingly fragmented.

Search engines. AI assistants. Communities. Social platforms. Video. Content platforms.

Businesses need a way to manage their reach across all of them.

coverMyGame - Indie Hackers

# coverMyGame

September 19, 2026 Why I am building coverMyGame

Most platforms that connect game developers with creators ask for a subscriber count or a quality bar before you can use them properly. Those are fair rules that happen to lock out everybody who is starting. This is the one I wanted when I started, and what I am trying to do differently. There are already plenty of places where game developers and creators find each other, and most of them work. I am not here to tell you they are broken. I am here because I could not get through the door of any of them when I started, and I doubt I am the only one.

## The bar is invisible once you are over it

Look at what most of these platforms ask for before you can use them properly. A subscriber count. A channel that has been going a while. On the other side, a game that clears somebody’s quality bar, with a trailer that looks like it had a budget and a store page that looks like a studio wrote it.

None of that is unfair. If you are running a service at scale, thresholds are how you keep the quality up and the noise down, and every one of those rules was written for a good reason. The trouble is that they are invisible to everybody already past them, and they are the entire experience if you are not.

A developer shipping their first game has no reviews to point at. A creator on their second month has no subscriber count to clear a floor with. Both of them are exactly the people who would get the most out of finding each other, and both of them are the people the rules are written to filter out.

## I hit this from both sides

I am building a YouTube channel myself, and starting was harder than I expected. Not the making: the getting anywhere near the games. Every route to a developer wanted a number I did not have yet. And the same week I would read a post from somebody who had just shipped a first game asking, in earnest, how on earth you get anyone to look at it.

So this is not market research. I am building the tool I wanted to use, and if it is useful to other people starting out then that is the whole of the ambition. Everything in it exists because it annoyed me first.

## The other half: being reachable should not cost this much

The flip side of being hard to reach is being too easy to reach. Once one address of yours is out there, you get PDFs. You get press kits you did not ask for. You get the same letter eleven times from eleven people who all bought the same list, and a few that are not letters at all but somebody trying to get into your account.

And the honest bit, which nobody says out loud: sometimes I do not want to talk to anybody. I want to look at what is there, take the thing I am interested in, and get on with it. Having to open a conversation with a stranger before anything can happen is a real cost, and for a lot of people it is the cost that stops them.

## So you decide how much of this you want

This is the part I care most about getting right. How much contact you accept is a setting, not a character trait, and both extremes are supported on purpose.

- Say what you actually want sent, and nothing outside it reaches you. If that is nothing at all, that works too, and it costs you nothing to say so.
- You never have to negotiate. A creator can look through the games here and ask for a key; a developer can say yes or nothing. No pitch meeting, no small talk, no thread.
- Or talk properly, if that is what you like. Some of the best coverage comes out of two people actually getting on. The point is that it is a choice you make, not a toll you pay.

## A feedback loop that goes both ways

The thing missing from almost every version of this is what happens afterwards. A developer sends a key into the dark and never learns whether the video happened, whether it landed, or why not. A creator covers a game and never hears whether it moved anything.

Both sides get to say what worked here, and both sides get to read it. Two people getting better at this beats two people guessing at it, and over enough rounds that is the thing that makes a small channel and a small studio worth each other’s time.

## It is not unique, and that is fine

I want to be straight about this, because a launch post that claims to have invented something is the first sign that it has not. This is not a new idea. Plenty of people are doing a version of it, and several of them are doing it well.

If there were one car maker in the world we would all still be driving the same car. Things get better because somebody builds the version they wanted and other people turn out to want it too. So: no corporate look, no corporate rules, a low front door, and someone at the other end who answers. I am flexible, I will take feedback seriously, and I would rather change my mind in public than defend a decision I have gone off. What is not built yet

It would be easy to write all of that as though the thing were finished. It is not, and pretending otherwise would break the first rule on the card above.

- I do think about how this pays for itself one day, but none of that is built: no checkout, no billing page, nothing to buy. Use the whole thing for free while that is true.
- I am still running interviews with developers and creators, and the answers still change what gets built next.

## Come and punk your way through this with me

That is genuinely how this feels: no publisher, no permission, no waiting to be picked. Building the room I wanted to be in, and leaving the door open.

Accounts are not open yet. Leave an address on the waiting list and I will write when they are. I may ask you for a short interview before then, and nothing else.

The system shares the same processing architecture as NKTg AI, with clearly defined roles between layers:

- NKTg AI: Handles logical processing, measures semantic energy, and decomposes and shapes the information structure before passing it on.

## 2. Distinct Operating Advantages

Unlike the Local model, which runs directly via WebAssembly on the device, LLM Cloud mode offers clear hardware advantages:

- No high-end device required: Users don't need a computer with powerful RAM, CPU, or GPU.
- Zero device load: The entire heavy language-generation process runs entirely on cloud infrastructure.

September 18, 2026 NKTg AI – LLM Local 

## 1. Functional Separation Architecture: Processing Brain and Execution Interface

In the NKTg AI – LLM Local architecture, the system clearly separates two independent functional layers to eliminate the drawbacks of monolithic language models:

- NKTg AI (Logical & Quantitative Processing Brain): Handles the core processing role. Using physical operators, the system measures semantic energy, performs structural decomposition, decodes information layers, and precisely extracts the Core Content. This layer determines the authenticity of the data, eliminating subjective inference entirely.
- LLM Local (Generative Interface): Converts the structure standardized by the NKTg AI "brain" into natural language. Rather than reasoning from raw data itself, this component performs text generation based on the already-shaped logical framework, ensuring fluency and effective communication with the user.

## 2. Advantages of Running LLM Local in the Browser via WebAssembly

Integrating and running LLM Local directly in the web browser through WebAssembly technology delivers outstanding strategic value:

- Absolute Data Security (Zero Data Leakage): The entire information-processing pipeline stays confined to the user's own device hardware, completely eliminating the risk of data leakage from transmission to external cloud servers.
- Minimal Latency (Low Latency): By leveraging local computing power directly through WebAssembly, the model responds instantly, eliminating delays caused by internet transmission.
- Offline Operation: The system maintains continuous, stable performance even when the device is completely disconnected from the internet.
- Optimized Hardware Utilization: WebAssembly executes code at near-native speed directly in the browser, making the most of available computing power without requiring complex software installation.

## 3. Decoding and Overcoming the Core Weaknesses of Traditional LLMs

The system is designed to eliminate the inherent weaknesses of standalone LLMs:

- Hallucination Mitigation: Traditional LLMs rely on statistical probability to generate tokens, creating a risk of fabricating information. With the filtering layer from NKTg AI, LLM Local only receives verified data, ensuring responses stay grounded in the source material.
- Context Focus Optimization: When processing complex text, NKTg AI isolates conditional/exceptional components (DAMP) from core actions (AMP), preventing information noise.
- Objective & Creative Synthesis: Precisely preserves the user's original intent and information while optimizing the AI's fluent, creative expression. This eliminates any tendency to distort data, ensuring output that is both professionally deep (legal, technical, financial) and naturally fluent.

## 4. Standard Operating Flow: Decode → Generate

# coverMyGame

September 19, 2026 Why I am building coverMyGame

Most platforms that connect game developers with creators ask for a subscriber count or a quality bar before you can use them properly. Those are fair rules that happen to lock out everybody who is starting. This is the one I wanted when I started, and what I am trying to do differently. There are already plenty of places where game developers and creators find each other, and most of them work. I am not here to tell you they are broken. I am here because I could not get through the door of any of them when I started, and I doubt I am the only one.

## The bar is invisible once you are over it

Look at what most of these platforms ask for before you can use them properly. A subscriber count. A channel that has been going a while. On the other side, a game that clears somebody’s quality bar, with a trailer that looks like it had a budget and a store page that looks like a studio wrote it.

None of that is unfair. If you are running a service at scale, thresholds are how you keep the quality up and the noise down, and every one of those rules was written for a good reason. The trouble is that they are invisible to everybody already past them, and they are the entire experience if you are not.

A developer shipping their first game has no reviews to point at. A creator on their second month has no subscriber count to clear a floor with. Both of them are exactly the people who would get the most out of finding each other, and both of them are the people the rules are written to filter out.

## I hit this from both sides

I am building a YouTube channel myself, and starting was harder than I expected. Not the making: the getting anywhere near the games. Every route to a developer wanted a number I did not have yet. And the same week I would read a post from somebody who had just shipped a first game asking, in earnest, how on earth you get anyone to look at it.

So this is not market research. I am building the tool I wanted to use, and if it is useful to other people starting out then that is the whole of the ambition. Everything in it exists because it annoyed me first.

## The other half: being reachable should not cost this much

The flip side of being hard to reach is being too easy to reach. Once one address of yours is out there, you get PDFs. You get press kits you did not ask for. You get the same letter eleven times from eleven people who all bought the same list, and a few that are not letters at all but somebody trying to get into your account.

And the honest bit, which nobody says out loud: sometimes I do not want to talk to anybody. I want to look at what is there, take the thing I am interested in, and get on with it. Having to open a conversation with a stranger before anything can happen is a real cost, and for a lot of people it is the cost that stops them.

## So you decide how much of this you want

This is the part I care most about getting right. How much contact you accept is a setting, not a character trait, and both extremes are supported on purpose.

- Say what you actually want sent, and nothing outside it reaches you. If that is nothing at all, that works too, and it costs you nothing to say so.
- You never have to negotiate. A creator can look through the games here and ask for a key; a developer can say yes or nothing. No pitch meeting, no small talk, no thread.
- Or talk properly, if that is what you like. Some of the best coverage comes out of two people actually getting on. The point is that it is a choice you make, not a toll you pay.

## A feedback loop that goes both ways

The thing missing from almost every version of this is what happens afterwards. A developer sends a key into the dark and never learns whether the video happened, whether it landed, or why not. A creator covers a game and never hears whether it moved anything.

Both sides get to say what worked here, and both sides get to read it. Two people getting better at this beats two people guessing at it, and over enough rounds that is the thing that makes a small channel and a small studio worth each other’s time.

## It is not unique, and that is fine

I want to be straight about this, because a launch post that claims to have invented something is the first sign that it has not. This is not a new idea. Plenty of people are doing a version of it, and several of them are doing it well.

If there were one car maker in the world we would all still be driving the same car. Things get better because somebody builds the version they wanted and other people turn out to want it too. So: no corporate look, no corporate rules, a low front door, and someone at the other end who answers. I am flexible, I will take feedback seriously, and I would rather change my mind in public than defend a decision I have gone off. What is not built yet

It would be easy to write all of that as though the thing were finished. It is not, and pretending otherwise would break the first rule on the card above.

- I do think about how this pays for itself one day, but none of that is built: no checkout, no billing page, nothing to buy. Use the whole thing for free while that is true.
- I am still running interviews with developers and creators, and the answers still change what gets built next.

## Come and punk your way through this with me

That is genuinely how this feels: no publisher, no permission, no waiting to be picked. Building the room I wanted to be in, and leaving the door open.

Accounts are not open yet. Leave an address on the waiting list and I will write when they are. I may ask you for a short interview before then, and nothing else.

People still search Google, but they also discover businesses through AI assistants, Reddit, YouTube, LinkedIn, Quora, Medium, communities, and other places across the web.

And this creates a messy problem for businesses.

You might have great content, but nobody sees it.

You might rank well on Google, but not appear in AI answers.

You might know exactly what content you need to create, but getting it distributed across the right channels is another problem.

You might discover an SEO issue, but fixing it requires another tool, another person, or a developer.

We think businesses need an OS for reach one place to manage how they get discovered across the modern web.

# Foca Upscaler

September 18, 2026 Higher resolution doesn’t always mean a better image

I've been working on Foca Upscaler for a while, and one problem kept coming back while testing low-resolution images:

Making an image sharper is easy. Recovering detail that is no longer there is much harder.

Traditional enhancement can clean up edges, reduce softness, and make an image look crisper. That works well when the original image already contains enough usable information.

But some images are simply missing too much detail.

A tiny face, compressed hair, fabric texture, or a blurred object doesn't suddenly contain more information just because you upscale it 4x.

That was the reason I added Physics mode to Foca.

Foca now has two different enhancement approaches.

Sharp is meant for images where the original structure is already there and mostly needs cleaner, clearer enlargement.

Physics is for images where more detail needs to be reconstructed rather than simply sharpened.

The interesting part is that reconstruction creates a completely different problem.

If you push it too far, the result can look impressive but stop being faithful to the original. Skin becomes too perfect. Fabric gains textures that may never have existed. Small details become sharper, but not necessarily more accurate.

So the goal with Physics isn't simply “generate as much detail as possible.”

It's to reconstruct enough detail to make a low-resolution image useful again without turning it into a different image.

That's also changed how I think about resolution.

Foca supports upscaling up to 16K, but 16K alone isn't a quality metric. If those extra pixels are filled with fake-looking detail, the larger image isn't really better.

For me, the harder problem is finding the point where reconstruction helps more than it hurts.

That's still one of the most interesting parts of building Foca.

# Foca Upscaler

September 18, 2026 Higher resolution doesn’t always mean a better image

I've been working on Foca Upscaler for a while, and one problem kept coming back while testing low-resolution images:

Making an image sharper is easy. Recovering detail that is no longer there is much harder.

Traditional enhancement can clean up edges, reduce softness, and make an image look crisper. That works well when the original image already contains enough usable information.

But some images are simply missing too much detail.

A tiny face, compressed hair, fabric texture, or a blurred object doesn't suddenly contain more information just because you upscale it 4x.

That was the reason I added Physics mode to Foca.

Foca now has two different enhancement approaches.

Sharp is meant for images where the original structure is already there and mostly needs cleaner, clearer enlargement.

Physics is for images where more detail needs to be reconstructed rather than simply sharpened.

The interesting part is that reconstruction creates a completely different problem.

If you push it too far, the result can look impressive but stop being faithful to the original. Skin becomes too perfect. Fabric gains textures that may never have existed. Small details become sharper, but not necessarily more accurate.

So the goal with Physics isn't simply “generate as much detail as possible.”

It's to reconstruct enough detail to make a low-resolution image useful again without turning it into a different image.

That's also changed how I think about resolution.

Foca supports upscaling up to 16K, but 16K alone isn't a quality metric. If those extra pixels are filled with fake-looking detail, the larger image isn't really better.

For me, the harder problem is finding the point where reconstruction helps more than it hurts.

That's still one of the most interesting parts of building Foca.

You've probably noticed your cable bill creeping up month after month, or maybe you're tired of paying for channels you never watch. IPTV offers a way to stream live TV and on-demand content over your internet connection, often at a fraction of traditional cable costs. But if you're new to how to get IPTV, the process can feel confusing—especially with so many providers, apps, and devices to choose from.

This guide walks you through the entire process from start to finish. You'll learn how to pick a provider, what equipment you need, and exactly how to set everything up on your preferred device. By the end, you'll be streaming your favorite channels without the guesswork.

## What You Need Before You Start

Before you dive into subscriptions and apps, make sure your internet connection can handle IPTV streaming. Most providers recommend at least 10 Mbps for standard definition and 25 Mbps or higher for HD content. If multiple people in your household stream simultaneously, you'll want even more bandwidth.

You'll also need a compatible device. IPTV works on Fire TV Stick, Android TV boxes, Smart TVs, smartphones, tablets, and computers. Pick the device you'll use most often—many people start with a Fire TV Stick because it's affordable and simple to configure.

Finally, decide whether you want a legal IPTV service or a grey-market option. Legal services like YouTube TV, Hulu + Live TV, and Sling TV operate with broadcaster licenses and offer reliable streams with customer support. Grey-market services are cheaper but come with risks including service interruptions, legal concerns, and no guarantees. This guide focuses on the general process that applies to both, but you should understand the tradeoffs.

## Step 1: Choose an IPTV Provider and Subscription Plan

Your first real decision is picking a provider. If you want a legitimate service with major networks like ESPN, CNN, and local channels, compare options like YouTube TV, Hulu + Live TV, Fubo, or Sling TV. These services charge $40 to $80 per month depending on the channel lineup.

If you're exploring other options, research providers carefully. Look for reviews, check how long they've been operating, and ask about trial periods. A 24-hour or 3-day trial lets you test stream quality and channel availability before committing. For a detailed comparison of providers, check out the best iptv subscription usa rankings.

When you subscribe, you'll typically receive login credentials (a username and password) and either an M3U URL or an app download link. Save these details somewhere secure—you'll need them for setup.

## Step 2: Decide How You'll Watch

How to use IPTV depends entirely on your device. Most people choose one of these four options:

Fire TV Stick is the most popular choice for beginners. It plugs into any HDMI port, connects to your Wi-Fi, and runs dedicated IPTV apps.

Smart TVs with Android TV, webOS, or Tizen can run IPTV apps directly without extra hardware. Check your TV's app store to see what's available.

Android boxes like Nvidia Shield or generic devices give you more control and customization options, but they cost more and require a bit more technical comfort.

Mobile devices and computers work well if you want to watch on the go or don't have a TV setup yet. Most providers offer iOS, Android, and web apps.

Pick the device that fits your household. If you're unsure, start with a Fire TV Stick—it's under $50 and works with nearly every provider.

## Step 3: Install the IPTV App on Your Device

Once you've chosen your device, how to install IPTV varies slightly depending on the platform.

### How to Get IPTV on Firestick

Plug your Fire TV Stick into your TV and complete the initial Amazon account setup. From the home screen, navigate to the search icon and type the name of your IPTV provider's app. If it's available in the Amazon App Store, download and install it directly.

For apps not in the official store, you'll need to enable installation from unknown sources. Go to Settings > My Fire TV > Developer Options, then turn on "Apps from Unknown Sources." Next, install the Downloader app from the Amazon App Store. Open Downloader, enter the URL your provider gave you, and download the APK file. Once it downloads, click Install.

After installation, open the app and enter your login credentials. The app will load your channel list and you're ready to watch.

# coverMyGame

September 19, 2026 Why I am building coverMyGame

Most platforms that connect game developers with creators ask for a subscriber count or a quality bar before you can use them properly. Those are fair rules that happen to lock out everybody who is starting. This is the one I wanted when I started, and what I am trying to do differently. There are already plenty of places where game developers and creators find each other, and most of them work. I am not here to tell you they are broken. I am here because I could not get through the door of any of them when I started, and I doubt I am the only one.

## The bar is invisible once you are over it

Look at what most of these platforms ask for before you can use them properly. A subscriber count. A channel that has been going a while. On the other side, a game that clears somebody’s quality bar, with a trailer that looks like it had a budget and a store page that looks like a studio wrote it.

None of that is unfair. If you are running a service at scale, thresholds are how you keep the quality up and the noise down, and every one of those rules was written for a good reason. The trouble is that they are invisible to everybody already past them, and they are the entire experience if you are not.

A developer shipping their first game has no reviews to point at. A creator on their second month has no subscriber count to clear a floor with. Both of them are exactly the people who would get the most out of finding each other, and both of them are the people the rules are written to filter out.

## I hit this from both sides

I am building a YouTube channel myself, and starting was harder than I expected. Not the making: the getting anywhere near the games. Every route to a developer wanted a number I did not have yet. And the same week I would read a post from somebody who had just shipped a first game asking, in earnest, how on earth you get anyone to look at it.

So this is not market research. I am building the tool I wanted to use, and if it is useful to other people starting out then that is the whole of the ambition. Everything in it exists because it annoyed me first.

## The other half: being reachable should not cost this much

The flip side of being hard to reach is being too easy to reach. Once one address of yours is out there, you get PDFs. You get press kits you did not ask for. You get the same letter eleven times from eleven people who all bought the same list, and a few that are not letters at all but somebody trying to get into your account.

And the honest bit, which nobody says out loud: sometimes I do not want to talk to anybody. I want to look at what is there, take the thing I am interested in, and get on with it. Having to open a conversation with a stranger before anything can happen is a real cost, and for a lot of people it is the cost that stops them.

## So you decide how much of this you want

This is the part I care most about getting right. How much contact you accept is a setting, not a character trait, and both extremes are supported on purpose.

- Say what you actually want sent, and nothing outside it reaches you. If that is nothing at all, that works too, and it costs you nothing to say so.
- You never have to negotiate. A creator can look through the games here and ask for a key; a developer can say yes or nothing. No pitch meeting, no small talk, no thread.
- Or talk properly, if that is what you like. Some of the best coverage comes out of two people actually getting on. The point is that it is a choice you make, not a toll you pay.

## A feedback loop that goes both ways

The thing missing from almost every version of this is what happens afterwards. A developer sends a key into the dark and never learns whether the video happened, whether it landed, or why not. A creator covers a game and never hears whether it moved anything.

Both sides get to say what worked here, and both sides get to read it. Two people getting better at this beats two people guessing at it, and over enough rounds that is the thing that makes a small channel and a small studio worth each other’s time.

## It is not unique, and that is fine

I want to be straight about this, because a launch post that claims to have invented something is the first sign that it has not. This is not a new idea. Plenty of people are doing a version of it, and several of them are doing it well.

If there were one car maker in the world we would all still be driving the same car. Things get better because somebody builds the version they wanted and other people turn out to want it too. So: no corporate look, no corporate rules, a low front door, and someone at the other end who answers. I am flexible, I will take feedback seriously, and I would rather change my mind in public than defend a decision I have gone off. What is not built yet

It would be easy to write all of that as though the thing were finished. It is not, and pretending otherwise would break the first rule on the card above.

- I do think about how this pays for itself one day, but none of that is built: no checkout, no billing page, nothing to buy. Use the whole thing for free while that is true.
- I am still running interviews with developers and creators, and the answers still change what gets built next.

## Come and punk your way through this with me

That is genuinely how this feels: no publisher, no permission, no waiting to be picked. Building the room I wanted to be in, and leaving the door open.

Accounts are not open yet. Leave an address on the waiting list and I will write when they are. I may ask you for a short interview before then, and nothing else.

## Solving the Four Most Common Setup Problems

Problem 1: "Invalid credentials" or login failure

Double-check username/password for typos. Ensure subscription is active by logging into your account on the provider's website. Some services require you to link your device MAC address in account settings.

Problem 2: Buffering or frozen streams

Test your internet speed at speedtest.net. If below 25 Mbps, lower stream quality in app settings. Restart your router. Connect device via ethernet instead of WiFi if possible. Close other bandwidth-heavy apps.

Problem 3: Missing channels or broken links

Providers update channel lists regularly. Check for app updates in your device's store. Some services require you to refresh your M3U playlist URL manually in settings. Contact provider support if specific channels remain unavailable for 24+ hours.

Problem 4: "App not compatible" on older devices

Devices older than 5-6 years may lack processing power for modern IPTV apps. Solution: Use a generic IPTV player like VLC (supports M3U playlists) or upgrade to a $30-40 streaming stick.

## Advanced Setup: Optimizing Performance

Once basic setup works, improve your experience with these adjustments:

Enable hardware acceleration: In app settings, turn on GPU decoding to reduce buffering and improve picture quality on supported devices.

Configure DNS settings: Some providers recommend specific DNS servers for faster stream loading. Switch your router or device DNS to Google (8.8.8.8) or Cloudflare (1.1.1.1) if provider doesn't specify.

Use a VPN selectively: A VPN adds privacy but can slow connections by 10-30%. Only use if your ISP throttles streaming traffic or you need to access geo-restricted content.

Schedule app updates: Enable automatic updates during off-hours (3-5 AM) to avoid interruptions during viewing.

External storage for recordings: If your IPTV app supports DVR functionality, connect a USB drive or external hard drive to store recorded content without filling device memory.

## What You Actually Need Before Subscribing

Your internet speed determines whether IPTV will work at all. For standard definition channels, you need at least 5 Mbps. HD channels require 10-15 Mbps per stream, and 4K content needs 25 Mbps or higher. If three people in your household plan to watch different channels simultaneously, multiply accordingly.

Run a speed test right now at your normal viewing time, not at 3 AM when nobody else is online. Most buffering complaints come from people who checked their speed once during off-peak hours and assumed that's what they'd always get.

You also need a compatible device. IPTV works on Amazon Fire Stick, Android boxes, Smart TVs with app support, smartphones, tablets, Windows PCs, and Macs. The device you already own probably works fine.
